description: Two political models, two technological ambitions, the same planet. Why the rivalry between **Beijing** and **Washington** structures the entire century.

hero.hook: In forty years, a country poorer than its neighbors has become the only credible rival of the United States.

blocks.text: The rivalry between **China** and **United States** has become the most important relationship of the 21st century. It is not just an economic race: it pits two political models, two technological ambitions and two visions of the world order against each other.

After the **Cold War**, the United States seemed without a serious rival. The meteoric rise of China has changed the situation. Some researchers today speak of **[[Thucydides Trap]]**: this situation, observed several times in history, where a rising power threatens to overtake an established power, making confrontation almost inevitable.

In 1978, China emerged exhausted from decades of internal unrest. Under the leadership of **Deng Xiaoping**, the country changed course and launched the “Four Modernizations”, breaking with communist orthodoxy to adopt a form of capitalism supervised by the Party.

The strategy is based on opening up to foreign capital. Special economic zones, of which **Shenzhen** became the symbol, attract businesses with tax advantages and cheap labor. China thus becomes “the factory of the world”.
China is the largest creditor of the United States: it holds approximately $800 billion in American debt. A brutal break would therefore ruin both economies at the same time.
Its entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 marked the start of an unprecedented expansion. In 2010, it overtook Japan and became the second largest economy in the world.

sections.title: From isolation to the world factory

blocks.text: The transition from cooperation to frank rivalry crystallized under the presidencies of **Donald Trump** and **Xi Jinping**. Washington accuses Beijing of unfair trade practices and technology theft, and imposes massive customs duties on Chinese products.

The real heart of the conflict is moving towards high technology. The Americans are seeking to isolate China from **semiconductors**, these chips essential to artificial intelligence and modern weaponry. It's called the [[Technological "decoupling"]].

Companies like Huawei or TikTok are seen by Washington as threats to national security. This policy continues even after Trump's departure, proof that the rivalry goes beyond American political divisions.

On the military level, the confrontation is moving towards Southeast Asia. Beijing claims almost the entire South China Sea, an area critical to global trade and rich in resources. To assert its sovereignty, China is transforming reefs into militarized artificial islands.

blocks.caption: Taiwan and the South China Sea have become the main point of military friction between Beijing and Washington.

blocks.text: The most sensitive point remains **Taiwan**. Beijing considers the island a rebel province to be reunified. Taiwan, however, benefits from growing support from the United States. A conflict in the strait would paralyze global maritime trade and the production of electronic chips, of which the island ensures high-end manufacturing.

Faced with this perceived encirclement, Xi Jinping is deploying the “New Silk Roads”, an investment project in more than 140 countries which allows China to secure its supplies and build an alternative network of influence vis-à-vis the West.

Beyond the numbers, this rivalry is also ideological. It contrasts the Western liberal model, based on democracy and human rights, with the Chinese model of rapid economic development led by a single party.

For many developing countries, Chinese efficiency offers an attractive alternative to Western aid, often conditional on respect for democracy. China is no longer content with integrating the international system: it is now seeking to reform it so that it better reflects its power.

This relationship enters a phase of systemic competition. The two countries are avoiding open war for the moment, but the emergence of a new technological **[[Cold War]]** seems difficult to avoid, forcing the rest of the world to position itself between these two power blocs.

In 1978, China was poorer than many developing countries. Forty years of record growth later, it has become the only power capable of challenging the United States on all fronts: economic, military and technological.
